opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that it doesn't really come down to how impressive the outputs look. Veo 3 can produce stunning video, and people see that and assume there must be something creative going on. But being able to generate novel-looking artifacts isn't the same thing as being creative in the deeper sense I care about, which is open-ended creativity: the ability to keep generating things that are genuinely new *and* interesting, and to build on those things to open up further possibilities nobody anticipated.

What determines whether a model can do that, I'd argue, is largely what's going on underneath, in its representation of the world. Two systems can produce identical outputs while having completely different internal structure. One might have what I'd call a unified, factored representation, where it actually understands things in a modular, sensible way, so that if you vary one concept the variation is meaningful. The other might have a fractured, entangled representation, where the same outputs are achieved by an enormous patchwork of special cases that happen to line up. On a benchmark you can't tell them apart. But when you ask them to go somewhere new, to extrapolate or to invent, they behave totally differently. The fractured one tends to fall apart or produce things that are novel in a shallow, recombinatory way.

And the way we train these models, with massive data and SGD toward a fixed objective, doesn't particularly encourage that clean, unified kind of representation. It gets you to the target, but the path it takes to the target matters a lot for creativity, and it's not a path that was shaped by open-ended discovery the way, say, evolution or human culture shaped our own understanding.

The other piece is what I'd call a sense of interestingness. A creative agent needs some intuition for what's worth doing next, not just what's plausible. Veo 3 is very good at plausible. It's trained to produce what the distribution says a video should look like given a prompt. But open-endedness requires stepping-stone thinking: recognizing that something weird or seemingly useless might be the doorway to something important later. That's not a thing you get from imitating the distribution. In fact, imitating the distribution kind of pulls you away from it.

So on its own, I'd say a model like that is a magnificent instrument for *human* creativity. The human brings the interestingness, the direction, the sense of what's worth exploring, and the model amplifies it. Whether it could be creative independently depends on whether we figure out how to give these systems better-structured representations and something like a genuine, autonomous sense of what's interesting. I think that's one of the most important open problems in the field, and frankly I don't think scaling alone is going to get us there.

r001.rationale: It says the human supplies interestingness, direction, and what is worth exploring, while the model amplifies that creativity.

r002.rationale: It connects internal representation to extrapolation and invention, and says the training path matters, but does not explain which possibilities are reachable through gradient following.

r003.rationale: It says fractured representations yield shallow recombination and may fail when asked to invent, while deeper open-ended creativity depends on a better-structured representation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that we have to be careful about what we mean by "creative." A model like Veo 3 can produce things that are novel in the sense that you've never seen that exact video before, and they can be very impressive, very beautiful even. But I'd distinguish that from creativity in the deeper sense, which is about open-endedness, about generating things that are genuinely new in a way that builds on what came before and leads somewhere interesting over time.

So the question becomes: what's the source of the novelty? With these models, it's largely interpolation within a distribution that was built from human creative output. The humans who made all those videos were the creative agents. The model is a kind of very sophisticated remixer of that creativity. That's not nothing, but it's not the same as the model itself having the capacity to step outside the distribution and go somewhere nobody's been.

What I think actually determines whether something can be genuinely creative on its own is whether it has a sense of interestingness, a way of recognizing that something is a stepping stone worth pursuing, even when it doesn't know where it leads. That's what we see in evolution, in human culture, in science. The great discoveries weren't the result of optimizing toward a known objective. They came from following what was interesting and accumulating stepping stones over a very long time. Those systems have their own internal compass for divergence.

A video model as it's typically deployed doesn't have that. It responds to a prompt, produces an output, and that's the end of the loop. There's no ongoing process where it's exploring, collecting its own discoveries, and building on them. If you wanted genuine autonomous creativity, you'd need to close that loop. You'd need the system to be able to generate, to evaluate what it generated in terms of interestingness rather than fitting a target, and then to keep going from there, indefinitely.

And there's a deeper point here too, which is about representation. I've argued that the way these models represent what they've learned is kind of a tangled mess internally, what I've called fractured entangled representation. Humans, when we really understand something, have a more modular, decomposed understanding of it. You can take an idea apart and recombine the pieces in new ways. That's a big part of how creativity works. If the model's internal representation doesn't afford that kind of recombination, then even if it looks like it's being creative, it's going to have trouble doing the sort of intentional, compositional novelty that real creators do.

So to summarize, I'd say it comes down to three things: whether the system can escape the distribution it was trained on, whether it has an internal sense of what's interesting that can drive open-ended exploration, and whether its representations are structured in a way that supports genuine recombination. Right now, I think these models are impressive mirrors of human creativity more than they are independent creative agents. But those aren't fundamental barriers. They're design choices, and they point to where the research needs to go.

r001.rationale: The response says the humans who made the training videos were the creative agents and describes the model as a remixer of their creativity.

r002.rationale: It links representation structure to recombination and compositional novelty, but does not explain which creative possibilities are reachable through gradient following.

r003.rationale: It says tangled representations hinder intentional, compositional novelty, but does not state that poor representation constrains transformative creativity more than derivative creativity.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is where the impetus for creating something comes from. A video model can produce something surprising, something nobody has seen before, and that’s interesting. But if we give it a prompt and then decide whether the result is good, we’re supplying a lot of the creative direction. We’re deciding what’s worth pursuing.

For it to be creative on its own, I’d want to see it participate in that process of discovery. Can it generate something, notice an unexpected possibility in what it generated, and decide to explore that possibility further? Could that exploration lead somewhere that wasn’t specified in the original request?

That’s where open-endedness becomes important. When you create, you don’t necessarily know what you’re trying to create at the beginning. Something you encounter changes your sense of what’s interesting. So I wouldn’t judge this entirely by how impressive an individual video looks. I’d look at whether the system can sustain a process in which its own discoveries change what it pursues next.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes the model’s production of surprising video from the human’s role in prompting it and deciding what is worth pursuing.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss internal world representations or gradient following.

r003.rationale: It does not compare how a poor representation constrains transformative versus derivative creativity.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the key question is where the ideas come from. A model can produce something surprising, something that none of us has seen before, and that’s interesting. But if a person is supplying the intention and selecting everything worth pursuing, then the creative process is distributed between the person and the model. That’s different from the model driving that process itself.

For me, “on its own” would mean that it can discover something interesting and decide to follow it, even when that takes it away from whatever we initially asked it to do. Can it recognize a stepping stone without knowing where that stepping stone leads? Can one thing it creates change what it wants to explore next?

That’s where open-endedness becomes important. Creativity isn’t just generating a really impressive artifact in one shot. It’s also the unfolding of a search, where the possibilities you encounter reshape the search itself. So I’d want to look beyond the quality of the videos and ask whether the system has an ongoing process of discovery. A beautiful output alone doesn’t settle that question.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes the person supplying intention and selecting ideas from the model generating outputs, and contrasts that shared process with the model driving discovery itself.

r002.rationale: It discusses discovery and open-ended search, but does not state that the model’s internal world representation determines which possibilities gradient following can reach.

r003.rationale: It does not compare how a poor underlying representation constrains transformative creativity versus derivative creativity.
